Metal hydrides (like sodium hydride, lithium aluminum hydride), metal alkyls (like trimethylaluminum, diethylzinc), metal aryls (like phenyllithium), and silanes (like silane, SiH4) are all known for their extreme reactivity with air. These compounds spontaneously ignite when exposed to air at room temperature without requiring an ignition source. This property classifies them as pyrophoric materials.

Pyrophoric materials are defined as substances that ignite spontaneously in air at or below 130°F (54.4°C) without requiring an external ignition source. This is distinct from:
- Highly flammable (which burn readily but require an ignition source)
- Combustible (which can burn but are less easily ignited than flammable materials)
- Nonflammable (which do not burn under normal conditions)

The compounds mentioned in the question - metal hydrides, metal alkyls, metal aryls, and silanes - all exhibit pyrophoric behavior due to their extreme reactivity with oxygen and moisture in the air, causing them to ignite spontaneously.
